terms.simpleDefinition: Your GPU's memory. Think of it like a desk — bigger models need bigger desks to work on.
terms.detailedDefinition: VRAM (Video Random Access Memory) is memory on your graphics card. When running AI models, the model needs to fit entirely in VRAM to run efficiently. More VRAM = can run larger models. If the model doesn't fit, it offloads to system RAM and runs slowly.
terms.example: A model needs 8GB of VRAM. Your RTX 3060 has 12GB. You're good.
terms.beginnerTip: Don't worry about the details — just know that more is better for running AI models.

terms.simpleDefinition: A compressed version of a model. It's like ZIPping a file — much smaller, almost the same quality.
terms.detailedDefinition: Quantization reduces the numbers inside a model from 16-bit (or 32-bit) to 4-bit precision. This shrinks the model by ~60% with only 1-3% quality loss. Q4_K_M is the most popular quantization — it balances size reduction with quality. Q5_K_M is slightly better quality, Q8_0 is near-lossless but much larger.
terms.example: A 7B model at full precision needs 14GB. At Q4_K_M it needs only 4-5GB — fitting on most GPUs.
terms.beginnerTip: Always use Q4_K_M unless someone tells you otherwise. It gives you the best quality-to-size ratio.

terms.simpleDefinition: Like an app store for AI models. One click to install any model. Made for beginners.
terms.detailedDefinition: Ollama is free software that lets you download and run AI models locally on your computer. It handles all the technical complexity — you just run simple commands like 'ollama pull qwen3:7b'. It works on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
terms.example: Open terminal, type: ollama pull qwen3:7b — and the AI model installs.
terms.beginnerTip: Use Ollama. It's the easiest way to run local AI models. Download from ollama.com.

terms.simpleDefinition: A special file format that makes AI models easy to run on your computer.
terms.detailedDefinition: GGUF (formerly GGML) is a file format designed specifically for running AI models on local hardware. It packages the model in a way that's optimized for consumer GPUs and CPUs. When you download a model for Ollama or LM Studio, it's usually in GGUF format.
terms.example: When you see 'Qwen3-7B-Q4_K_M.gguf' — that's the GGUF file containing the compressed model.
terms.beginnerTip: You don't need to understand GGUF — Ollama handles it automatically.

terms.simpleDefinition: How big a model is. The number is how many tiny calculations it has. Bigger = smarter but needs more power.
terms.detailedDefinition: The number (7B, 14B, 70B) refers to how many parameters (tiny weights) the model has. A 7B model has 7 billion parameters. Larger models are generally more capable but need more VRAM. 7B fits on most modern GPUs. 14B needs 10-12GB VRAM. 70B needs 40GB+ (usually cloud).
terms.example: 7B = laptop, 14B = desktop, 70B = server room. Start small, upgrade as needed.
terms.beginnerTip: Start with a 7B model. Most people don't need bigger — the difference is small compared to the hardware jump.

terms.simpleDefinition: How much the AI can read at once. Like memory — longer context means it can see more of your conversation or documents.
terms.detailedDefinition: Context length is measured in tokens (roughly 1 token = 1 word). A model with 8K context can handle about 6,000 words at once — a long article or several pages of code. More context lets you paste in long documents or have very long conversations. But longer context uses more VRAM.
terms.example: 8K context = a long article. 32K = a short book. 128K = thick novel.
terms.beginnerTip: Start with whatever the default is. Increase it only if you need to analyze long documents.

terms.simpleDefinition: How fast the AI responds. Higher = snappier conversation. 20+ tok/s feels like instant chat.
terms.detailedDefinition: Tokens per second measures how quickly the AI generates text. 5-10 tok/s feels slow and sluggish. 20-40 tok/s is smooth and interactive. 50+ tok/s feels instantaneous. Speed depends on your GPU, model size, and quantization level.
terms.example: On an RTX 3060: Qwen 7B runs at 30-50 tok/s. On a MacBook M1: 15-25 tok/s.
terms.beginnerTip: Don't obsess over this number. As long as it's above 15 tok/s, the experience is good.

terms.simpleDefinition: A smart model that only uses part of itself for each task — but it still needs all parts in memory.
terms.detailedDefinition: Mixture of Experts (MoE) models have many specialized 'expert' sub-networks. For each query, only a few experts activate — making inference faster in compute terms. BUT all experts must still be stored in VRAM, so MoE doesn't save memory. GLM-4.7 Flash 30B is a popular MoE model.
terms.example: MoE is like having a team of specialists. Only the relevant ones answer each question, but you pay to keep all of them on retainer.
terms.beginnerTip: Don't special-case MoE models in your head — treat their VRAM requirements like any other model of similar size.

terms.simpleDefinition: The AI brain. It's a very large file of math that has learned to understand and generate text from reading billions of pages of the internet.
terms.detailedDefinition: A language model is a neural network trained on text data. After training on massive datasets, it can understand questions and generate responses. 'Local AI' means running this model on YOUR computer instead of paying a company to run it for you.
terms.example: Qwen 3 7B is a model. GPT-4 is a model. The difference is: one runs on your machine, one runs on OpenAI's servers.
terms.beginnerTip: Think of a model like a person who has read a lot and can answer questions. Smaller models are like enthusiastic interns. Larger models are like experts.

terms.simpleDefinition: When the model is too big for your GPU's memory, part of it spills over to regular RAM — and runs much slower.
terms.detailedDefinition: If your model doesn't fit in VRAM, parts of it get moved to system RAM. This is called offloading. The model still works, but generation slows from 30+ tok/s to 3-5 tok/s — making it barely usable. The fix is using a smaller model or smaller quantization.
terms.example: You try to run a 14B model on a 6GB GPU. It offloads to CPU. What took 0.5 seconds now takes 5 seconds.
terms.beginnerTip: If your AI is running extremely slowly, it's probably offloading to CPU. Switch to a smaller model or Q4_K_M quantization.

terms.simpleDefinition: A friendly chat interface for Ollama. Makes local AI feel like ChatGPT — just type and get answers.
terms.detailedDefinition: Open WebUI is a free, open-source web interface that connects to Ollama. Instead of using the terminal, you get a clean chat UI where you can conversationally interact with your models. It supports chat history, multiple models, and easy switching between them.
terms.example: Download Ollama, run it, then download Open WebUI — you get a ChatGPT-like experience running entirely on your computer.
terms.beginnerTip: If you want something that looks like ChatGPT, use Open WebUI on top of Ollama.

terms.simpleDefinition: A polished app for downloading and running AI models. Good for people who prefer clicking over typing.
terms.detailedDefinition: LM Studio is a free desktop app (Mac, Windows, Linux) that makes running local AI models easy. It has a built-in model browser, chat interface, and OpenAI-compatible server. It's more polished than Ollama's default UI but works similarly. Commercial use requires a paid license.
terms.example: Open LM Studio, search for 'Qwen 3', download, click 'Chat' — you're talking to your private AI.
terms.beginnerTip: Use Ollama if you're comfortable with a terminal. Use LM Studio if you prefer clicking.

terms.simpleDefinition: What you type to the AI. Better prompts get better answers — just like asking a person better questions.
terms.detailedDefinition: A prompt is the input you give to the AI model. The quality of your prompt dramatically affects output quality. Basic prompt: 'Write code.' Better prompt: 'Write a Python function that reads a CSV file and returns the average of a column named 'price', with error handling for missing values.'
terms.example:
Bad prompt: 'help with python'
Good prompt: 'Write a Python function that takes a list of numbers and returns their median, handling the case where the list is empty.'
terms.beginnerTip: Be specific and clear in your prompts. The AI can't read your mind — but it can do almost anything if you explain it clearly.

terms.simpleDefinition: A way for programs to talk to AI models. Lets you connect local AI to other tools and apps.
terms.detailedDefinition: An API (Application Programming Interface) lets software connect to AI models programmatically. Ollama runs a local API server on port 11434. This means you can connect your own apps, scripts, or services to your local AI — just like connecting to ChatGPT's API, but it's free and private.
terms.example: Your note-taking app connects to your local Ollama API. Every note gets automatically summarized using your private AI.
terms.beginnerTip: You don't need to understand APIs to use local AI. But once you're comfortable, connecting AI to your tools is where the magic happens.
